newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ fund managers welcome prospect of GPS float.
newsitem.headline: NZ fund managers welcome prospect of GPS float.

text.p: A sharemarket float of Government Property Services would be timely and create plenty of interest from institutions, leading fund managers told Wellington's Evening Post newspaper.
Treasurer Winston Peters signalled in the budget last week that the coalition Government was investigating the sale of GPS and Vehicle Testing New Zealand.
On Friday, Finance Minister Bill Birch said GPS could be floated on the sharemarket.
National Mutual's chief investment manager, Barry Lindsay, said a share float of GPS soon would be favourable because the outlook for commercial property in Auckland and Wellington was good.
"Property rents are beginning to firm, vacancies are falling (increasing demand) and are predicted to continue falling in Auckland and Wellington," Lindsay said.
He said the size of GPS would make it an attractive float. GPS has property investments worth NZ$260 million and its net worth was estimated to be $177 million in the budget.
Lindsay said listing GPS made good sense because it would be more difficult to sell all of its 36 properties individually.

About 80 percent of GPS assets are in Wellington, where it owns 10 buildings. Wellington properties include Bowen House, Defence House, 3 The Terrace, the Charles Ferguson, Bowen State, William Clayton and Freyberg buildings, St Paul's Square and the State Services Commission building.
Provincial centres with GPS properties include Tauranga, Gisborne, Napier, Hastings, Palmerston North, Wanganui, New Plymouth, Taumarunui, Kawerau, Nelson and Blenheim.
National Mutual would consider a stake in GPS as a listed company but only after examining the SOE's leases on buildings and how it was priced to the market if it were to be floated, Lindsay said.
Colonial investment manager Tim Mitchell said his company would consider GPS as an investment if listed.
AMP's chief property manager, Steve Swain, said there was a shortage of good property stocks on the sharemarket. He would be looking for more detail on GPS's assets.

Institutions increasingly appear to be buying shares in listed property companies instead of directly owning properties investments. This gives institutions liquidity, meaning they can sell their shares more readily.
Another advantage for institutions is the ability to see each day the value of the investment on the sharemarket, which makes investment decisions on buying or selling shares easier.
